entries.title: Resting on a citation checks what it says
entries.body: In your own articles, rest the pointer on a citation to a single work and, after about two seconds, its card asks "Does it say that?" by itself: does that work say what the paragraph claims? The answer appears in the card as it is written, and is kept as a chat you can carry on in Chat, so coming back to it does not ask again. It never starts on a tap; if the day's shared allowance of automatic checks runs out, the button still works.

entries.title: See how long you have spent reading
entries.body: An article's Metadata page shows Time spent reading, under Your reading: roughly how long you have spent in that article, in seconds, minutes or hours. It appears only on your own articles.

entries.title: Chats link to earlier chats; leaving closes them
entries.body: When a chat answer mentions an earlier chat on the same article, it links to it. A chat begun from a marked quiz answer is labelled in Chat's list, and the mark reopens it rather than starting another. Moving to any mode but Chat closes the open chat, which Back reopens, and an unsent question about a passage is kept.

entries.title: Figures and tables link to the original page
entries.body: Figures, tables and other media in an article added from a web address carry a small link back to the original page, to the same spot where the app can find it, or to the page itself otherwise. PDFs keep their own control.

entries.title: Repeated glossary terms are underlined more faintly
entries.body: The dotted underline under a glossary term grows fainter each time the term comes up again, so a word used all through a paper no longer carries the same strong mark every time. Point at it and the underline shows in full, with its definition as before.

entries.title: New guidance for Summary links and chat examples
entries.body: Summary is now asked to link each paragraph to the passages in the body that argue its point, rather than to the abstract or opening summary. In chats, the AI is asked for the clearest example or analogy, not one from your job or field just because it is yours.

entries.title: Boxed passages in arXiv papers keep their text
entries.body: Some arXiv papers set passages in titled boxes, and these could arrive as empty frames. They now come in with their title and text, and any pictures inside. This applies to articles added or processed again from now on; one already in your library does not change by itself.

entries.title: Dictation asks for the microphone as you press
entries.body: In Safari on iPad and iPhone, and other browsers not built on Chrome's engine, dictation could ask for permission to use the microphone again each time. It now asks the moment you press the dictate button, in chat and in the Feedback box, rather than a moment later, which is the likely cause.
